mainTopic: Court proceedings without the litigant present: testimony against a minor, hearing witnesses, confirming a שטר, and the steps before an אדרכתא
overview: The amud opens by finishing רבי ירמיה's case over a field held by a minor whose father had owned it. רבי אבין objects that witnesses cannot testify against a minor, who counts as absent. A ברייתא and סומכוס are debated. רבי אבהו brings a proof from a child who grabbed a field, but the גמרא rejects it, because our minor has his father's חזקה. The גמרא then discusses hearing witnesses without the litigant present: רבי יוחנן allows it only in urgent cases, and שמואל only once the case was opened and the defendant refused to come. רב and רבי יוחנן argue about confirming a שטר without the litigant, and רבא rules that it may be confirmed. The borrower still gets time to bring witnesses, then a ninety-day פתיחא, and only after that an אדרכתא. The אדרכתא covers land only, and the borrower is notified if he is nearby. The amud ends with רבינא's rules about trusting the court's messenger and passing a summons through a woman or neighbors, a limit that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Can witnesses testify when the minor is not legally present?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין finishes his objection: a court does not accept witnesses in the absence of the בעל דין, and a קטן counts as absent.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Do we accept witnesses] in the absence of a litigant?!
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes רבי אבין's objection to רבי ירמיה. Testimony against the minor should not be accepted, because a minor is not considered legally present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A minor cannot stand in court as a litigant. So taking testimony against him is like taking testimony with the other side missing, and רבי אבין assumes that is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A litigant, one of the sides in a court case

steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not where the minor is standing. A קטן does not count legally as a litigant, so even if he is there, it is as if the other side is missing.

phrases.english: in the absence of a litigant?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the objection that began before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: Accepting רבי ירמיה's witnesses against the minor
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Testimony is not accepted when the בעל דין is absent, and a minor counts as absent

steps.title: Minors who inherit stolen goods must pay
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה challenges the objection from a ברייתא that obligates both adult and minor heirs to return stolen property.
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we not? But it is taught: whether they are adults or minors, they are obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה fights back. A ברייתא obligates even minor heirs to return what their father stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If minors must pay, the court must be hearing testimony about the theft even though the minors cannot act as litigants. That suggests testimony against minors is accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: And do we not?
But isn't it taught:
whether adults or minors, they are obligated!
phrases.notes: This is about children who inherited stolen goods from their father. They have to give them back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counter-challenge to the objection in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that testimony against minors is not accepted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא obligates minor heirs to pay, which requires accepting testimony about them

steps.title: סומכוס disagrees with that ruling
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין answers that the ברייתא is disputed by סומכוס, who exempts the minors.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The dispute of סומכוס is at your side.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבין pushes back on רבי ירמיה's proof. סומכוס argues on that ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since סומכוס exempts minors, the ברייתא is not agreed by everyone. So it cannot force the court to accept testimony against a minor.

keyTerms.meaning: At your side, right next to your source

phrases.english: He said to him:
the dispute of Sumakhos is right at your side.
phrases.notes: סומכוס disagrees with that very ruling and holds that the minors don't have to pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 2
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא is disputed by סומכוס, so it is not a settled rule

steps.title: Is everyone following סומכוס just to take my field?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה protests that the court is suddenly following a minority view just to rule against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Did the whole world go to the trouble of standing with סומכוס just to take away what is mine?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה complains with a sharp rhetorical question. Why rely on סומכוס only in his case?
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס is a lone opinion, and the הלכה usually follows the majority who obligate minors. רבי ירמיה argues that switching to סומכוס here is unfair.

keyTerms.meaning: Went to the trouble, bent over backward

phrases.english: He said:
Did the whole world go to the trouble
and stand with Sumakhos
just to take away what is mine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי אבין's reliance on סומכוס
steps.kashyaTarget: Relying on סומכוס to rule against רבי ירמיה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: סומכוס is a minority view, so there is no reason to follow him only in this case

steps.title: רבי אבהו: a child who seizes a field loses it right away
steps.stepSummary: The case reaches רבי אבהו, who quotes רבי אושעיא: a child who grabs another's field has it taken from him at once, and he can bring witnesses when he grows up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile the matter came before רבי אבהו. He said: Have you not heard what רב יוסף בר חמא said in the name of רבי אושעיא? A child who took over his fellow's field with his slaves and said 'It is mine' — we do not wait until he grows up. We take it from him immediately, and when he grows up he can bring witnesses and we will see.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו brings a proof that supports רבי ירמיה. A court does not have to wait for a child to grow up before ruling against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי אושעיא's case the court acts against a minor right away. He keeps the right to bring witnesses later. רבי אבהו applies this to say רבי ירמיה can get the field now.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter rolled along and spread
We take it out of his possession

phrases.english: Meanwhile the matter rolled along,
and came before Rabbi Abbahu.
He said: Have you not heard
this teaching of Rav Yosef bar Chama
that he said in the name of Rabbi Oshaya?
For Rav Yosef bar Chama said
that Rabbi Oshaya said:
A child who took over with his slaves,
phrases.notes: He used his slaves to grab the field.

phrases.english: and went down into his fellow's field
and said, 'It is mine,'
we do not say: let us wait until he grows up;
rather, we take it out of his hands immediately,
and when he grows up, he may bring witnesses and we will see!

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא שְׁמִיעַ לְכוּ הָא דְּרַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source that supports רבי ירמיה's side
steps.raayaObject: That a court may rule against a minor now, without waiting for him to grow up
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אושעיא's ruling about a child who seized a field

steps.title: Not comparable: that child had no חזקה from his father
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבי אבהו's proof. That child is removed because he has no claim through his father. A minor holding his father's field keeps it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it comparable? There we take it from him because he has no חזקה from his father. But where he has his father's חזקה, we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes aside רבי אבהו's proof. The two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child in רבי אושעיא's case grabbed a field with no family claim, so he has nothing to stand on. The minor in our case holds his father's field and has his father's חזקה. So the field is not taken from him until he can argue his case.

keyTerms.meaning: A presumption of ownership coming from his father

steps.whatToRemember: A minor who holds land with his father's חזקה is not removed from it. A minor who just grabs land is removed at once.

phrases.english: Is it comparable?
There is where we take it from him
because he does not stand on a presumption from his father;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ חֲזָקָה דַּאֲבוּהּ, לָא.
phrases.english: but where he has his father's presumption, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? הָתָם הוּא דְּמַפְּקִינַן מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 5
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between רבי אושעיא's case and רבי ירמיה's case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The minor in our case has חזקה from his father, and the child in רבי אושעיא's case did not

steps.title: רבי שבתאי: witnesses may be accepted without the litigant present
steps.stepSummary: A new topic: רב אשי quotes רבי שבתאי, who rules that a court accepts witnesses even without the בעל דין present.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said in the name of רבי שבתאי: We accept witnesses in the absence of a litigant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new discussion about the rule that came up above. רבי שבתאי says witnesses can be accepted even when the other side is not there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Above, רבי אבין assumed that testimony needs the other side present, while רבי ירמיה's ברייתא seemed to point the other way. This statement says, as a general rule, that witnesses may be heard without him.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַבִּי שַׁבְּתַאי:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said that Rabbi Shabbtai said:

phrases.aramaic: מְקַבְּלִין עֵדִים שֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בַּעַל דִּין.
phrases.english: We accept witnesses in the absence of a litigant.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַבִּי שַׁבְּתַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion of the rule raised in step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony may be accepted even when the litigant is not present

steps.title: רבי יוחנן is surprised by this ruling
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן wonders how a court could accept witnesses without the litigant present.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן wondered about it: Do we really accept witnesses in the absence of a litigant?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן challenges רבי שבתאי's ruling with surprise. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן assumes testimony requires the other side to be present. רבי שבתאי's ruling goes against that basic assumption, so it needs to be explained.

keyTerms.meaning: He wondered at it, he was puzzled

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan wondered at it,
and do we really accept witnesses
in the absence of a litigant?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in step 7
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Testimony should require the litigant to be present

steps.title: The narrow case where witnesses are heard without the defendant
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא learned from רבי יוחנן that witnesses are accepted without the בעל דין only in an urgent case: the plaintiff or his witnesses are sick or about to travel, and the defendant was called but did not come.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא received this from him: for example, the plaintiff was sick, or his witnesses were sick, or his witnesses wanted to travel overseas, and the court sent for the defendant and he did not come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבי יוחנן's question from the last step. It describes the special case where a court may hear witnesses without the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן was surprised that a court would hear witnesses without the litigant. The answer is that this happens only when the testimony might be lost, through sickness or travel, and the defendant was called and chose not to come. Both conditions together make it fair to go ahead.

keyTerms.meaning: He received it from him, meaning he learned it as a teaching
Overseas, literally 'the country of the sea'

steps.whyThisMatters: This turns a surprising rule into a limited emergency rule. The court is protecting testimony that could be lost, and only after the defendant has been called.

phrases.aramaic: קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina received it from him:
phrases.notes: 'From him' means from רבי יוחנן, who asked the question in the last step.

phrases.english: For example, where he was sick
phrases.notes: 'He' is the one bringing the case, the plaintiff.

phrases.english: or his witnesses were sick,
or his witnesses wished
to travel overseas,
and they sent for him and he did not come.
phrases.notes: Here 'him' is the other side, the defendant, whom the court called.

steps.triggerLanguage: קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוחנן's wonder in step 8 by narrowing רבי שבתאי's ruling from step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ruling to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed that courts always hear witnesses without the litigant, which looks unfair.
steps.terutzMaskana: It happens only when the testimony may be lost and the defendant was called but refused to come.

steps.title: שמואל rules that witnesses may be heard without the litigant
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: a court accepts witnesses even when the בעל דין is not there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: we accept witnesses not in the presence of the litigant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling on the same subject, this time from שמואל. It sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On its own, שמואל's ruling sounds very broad, as if the court never needs the other side present. The next step will show that שמואל meant it in a limited way.

keyTerms.meaning: A litigant, a side in a court case
We accept witnesses, meaning the court hears their testimony

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
We accept witnesses
not in the presence of a litigant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ruling from שמואל on the same topic as רבי שבתאי in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A court may hear witnesses without the litigant present.

steps.title: מר עוקבא explains that שמואל meant an already-opened case
steps.stepSummary: מר עוקבא heard from שמואל himself that the rule applies only if the case was already opened and the defendant was called but did not come. If the case was not opened yet, the defendant can say he wants the בית דין הגדול.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר עוקבא said: שמואל explained it to me himself. It means a case where the court already opened his case, sent for him, and he did not come. But if they did not open the case yet, he can say: I am going to the בית דין הגדול.
steps.whatsHappening: מר עוקבא gives an inside explanation of what שמואל meant. He limits the ruling to cases the local court has already started.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before a case is opened, the defendant may choose to be judged in the higher court, so skipping the local court is not refusing to appear. Once the case is opened and he still does not come, the court can go ahead and hear the witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: It was explained to me personally
They opened the case for him, meaning the court started the case
The High Court, a higher and more important court

phrases.english: Mar Ukva said:
To me personally it was explained by Shmuel himself:
For example, where they opened his case for him,
and they sent for him and he did not come.
But if they did not open the case for him,
he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The defendant is answering the person suing him.

phrases.english: I am going to the High Court.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא, לְדִידִי מִיפָּרְשָׁא לִי מִינֵּיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows שמואל's broad ruling from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses are heard without the defendant only if the case was already opened and he refused to come. Before that, he may insist on the בית דין הגדול.

steps.title: Why can't he ask for the High Court even after the case is opened?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the defendant may push the case to the בית דין הגדול, he should be able to do that even after the case was opened.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even when they opened the case for him, he can still say: I am going to the בית דין הגדול!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges מר עוקבא's line between an opened case and an unopened one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the right to go to the higher court is a real right, it should not disappear just because the local court started the case. So his not coming would still not count as refusing, and the witnesses should not be heard.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, a phrase that opens a challenge

phrases.english: If so,
even when they opened it for him,
he can say to him:
I am going to the High Court!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, כִּי פָתְחוּ לֵיהּ נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the distinction מר עוקבא drew in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר עוקבא's line between an opened case and an unopened one
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The defendant's right to go to the בית דין הגדול should apply at any time, so opening the case should make no difference.

steps.title: רבינא: the local court has a license from the High Court
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that we are talking about a local court holding written permission from the בית דין הגדול, so the defendant cannot move the case there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: for example, where the local court holds a license from the בית דין הגדול.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge by describing the exact situation where the defendant cannot ask for the higher court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the בית דין הגדול itself gave the local court permission to judge, going to the higher court gains him nothing. So once the case is opened and he does not come, he is simply refusing, and the court may hear the witnesses.
steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not saying a defendant can never ask for the בית דין הגדול. He is explaining the case שמואל was talking about, where the local court already has permission from it.
steps.whatToRemember: Witnesses are heard without the defendant when the case is opened, the court has permission from the בית דין הגדול, and the defendant was called and did not come.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
For example, where it holds a license
phrases.notes: The local court has a written permit letting it judge the case.

phrases.english: from the High Court.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: כְּגוֹן דְּנָקֵט דִּיסְקָא מִבֵּית דִּין הַגָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The defendant could always delay by asking for the בית דין הגדול, even after the case was opened.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the local court holds a license from the בית דין הגדול, he cannot move an opened case there, so his absence counts as refusing.

steps.title: רב and רבי יוחנן argue about confirming a שטר without the litigant
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a court may confirm a שטר without the בעל דין present. רבי יוחנן rules that it may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: we confirm a document not in the presence of the litigant. And רבי יוחנן said: we do not confirm a document not in the presence of the litigant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a related question: can a court confirm a שטר without the other side present? It brings an argument between רב and רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the topic was hearing witnesses. Now it is קיום שטר, confirming that the signatures on a document are real. רב allows it without the litigant, and רבי יוחנן requires him to be there.

keyTerms.meaning: A legal document, such as a loan document
We confirm the document, meaning the court checks that the signatures are real

phrases.english: Rav said:
We ratify a document
phrases.notes: The court confirms that the signatures on the document are real.

phrases.english: not in the presence of a litigant.
And Rabbi Yochanan said:
We do not ratify a document
not in the presence of a litigant.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: מְקַיְּימִין אֶת הַשְּׁטָר שֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בַּעַל דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from hearing witnesses to the related question of confirming a שטר without the litigant.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: a שטר may be confirmed without the litigant. רבי יוחנן: it may not.

steps.title: רב ששת explains רבי יוחנן's reason from the ox פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that רבי יוחנן learns from the פסוק about a goring ox: the owner must come and stand by his ox. So a litigant must be present.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to רבי יוסי בר אבהו: I will explain רבי יוחנן's reason to you. The פסוק says, 'And warning has been given to its owner and he has not guarded it.' The תורה is saying: let the owner of the ox come and stand by his ox.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת gives the source for רבי יוחנן's view from the previous step, using a פסוק about an ox that gores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'בבעליו' (to its owner) teaches that the warning testimony about a goring ox must be given in front of the owner. רבי יוחנן applies this to every case: testimony that affects a person, like confirming a שטר against him, must happen in his presence.

keyTerms.meaning: I will explain it to you
And warning was given to its owner
He should stand by his ox

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives רבי יוחנן's view a תורה source. It also explains why רבי יוחנן was surprised in step 8 that witnesses could be heard without the litigant.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said to Rabbi Yosei bar Abahu:
I will explain to you Rabbi Yochanan's reason:
The verse says:
"And warning has been given to its owner and he has not guarded it,"
The Torah said:
Let the owner of the ox come,
and stand by his ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבי יוחנן's view in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's rule that a שטר is not confirmed without the litigant
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 21:29, 'והועד בבעליו': testimony against an ox must be given in front of its owner

steps.title: רבא rules that a document may be confirmed without the litigant
steps.stepSummary: רבא decides the argument in favor of רב: a court may confirm a שטר even when the בעל דין is not there, and even if he protests loudly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is that we confirm a שטר without the other side being present, even if he stands there and screams.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא settles the disagreement from Step 14 between רב and רבי יוחנן, and he rules like רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן required the litigant to be present, based on the goring-ox פסוק. רבא rules that confirming the signatures does not need him there. His protest does not stop the process, though the next step shows he still gets a fair chance to fight the שטר.

keyTerms.meaning: Confirming a document by checking that its witnesses' signatures are real

steps.confusionAlert: Confirming the שטר does not mean the borrower loses his rights. As the next steps show, he can still bring witnesses to challenge it.

phrases.english: Rava said: The halacha is:
we confirm the document
not in the presence of the litigant,
and even if he stands and screams.
phrases.notes: He is screaming that the שטר is fake, and the court still goes ahead and confirms it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the disagreement of Steps 14–15 against רבי יוחנן's view.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows רב: a שטר may be confirmed without the בעל דין present, even over his protest.

steps.title: Giving the borrower time to bring witnesses
steps.stepSummary: If the borrower asks for time to bring witnesses against the שטר, the court gives it, and then adds three more court days.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says: 'Give me time until I bring witnesses to knock down this שטר,' we give him time. If he comes with them, fine. If not, we wait for him another Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains what happens after the שטר is confirmed when the borrower says he can prove it is no good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower gets a set amount of time to bring his witnesses. If he misses it, he still gets three more court sessions. The court is careful not to make him pay too fast.

phrases.english: And if he said: Set a time for me
until I bring witnesses
and I discredit the document,
we set a time for him.
If he came, he came,
phrases.notes: If he shows up with his witnesses, the court simply hears them.

phrases.english: if he did not come, we wait for him
Monday, Thursday, and Monday;
phrases.notes: These were the days the court was in session.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the procedure that follows רבא's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower who asks for time to discredit the שטר gets it, plus Monday, Thursday, and Monday.

steps.title: The ninety-day ban and its three waiting periods
steps.stepSummary: If he still does not come, the court issues a פתיחא for ninety days and does not touch his property, giving a reason for each thirty-day period.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he still does not come, we write a ban against him for ninety days. In the first thirty days we do not touch his property, because maybe he is busy borrowing money. In the middle thirty, maybe he could not find a loan and is busy selling property. In the last thirty, maybe the buyer is busy getting the money together.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא describes the next stage: a ninety-day ban during which the court still does not collect from his property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each thirty days has its own reason. The first is for borrowing, the second is for selling property, and the third is for the buyer to gather the payment. The ban puts pressure on him, but the court still assumes he may be honestly trying to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: A written ban (נידוי) against someone who will not come to court
We go down to his property, meaning we collect from it

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא אֲתָא – כָּתְבִינַן פְּתִיחָא עִלָּוֵיהּ
phrases.english: If he did not come, we write a ban against him
for ninety days.
The first thirty,
we do not go down to his property,
because we say: he is busy with money and will borrow.
The middle ones as well,
we do not go down to his property,
because one says: perhaps he did not find someone to borrow from,
and he is busy selling.
The last ones as well, we do not go down to his property,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: לוֹקֵחַ גּוּפֵיהּ קָא טָרַח בְּזוּזֵי.
phrases.english: because one says: the buyer himself is busy getting the money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לָא אֲתָא – כָּתְבִינַן פְּתִיחָא עִלָּוֵיהּ תִּשְׁעִין יוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next stage after the Monday-Thursday-Monday wait runs out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ninety-day ban is issued, and no property is taken during it, with a separate reason for each thirty days.

steps.title: After ninety days the court authorizes collection
steps.stepSummary: If he still does not come after ninety days, the court writes an אדרכתא on his property.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not come, we write an אדרכתא on his property.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the final stage: the lender is now given court permission to collect from the borrower's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every reason to wait has now been used up. The אדרכתא lets the lender go after the borrower's property to collect what he is owed.

keyTerms.meaning: A court document letting the creditor track down and take the debtor's property

phrases.english: If he did not come, we write an authorization on his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final result after the ninety days pass.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After ninety days with no response, an אדרכתא is written on his property.

steps.title: No waiting if he says he will not come
steps.stepSummary: The whole waiting process applies only if he said 'I am coming.' If he said 'I am not coming,' we write the אדרכתא right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when he said 'I am coming.' But if he said 'I am not coming,' we write it immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא limits the long waiting process: it only protects someone who says he plans to come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court waits because it assumes he is trying to deal with the case. Once he openly refuses, there is no reason to wait, so the אדרכתא is written at once.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply only to... (a limiting phrase)

phrases.english: And this applies when he said 'I am coming,'
but if he said 'I am not coming,'
we write it immediately.
phrases.notes: He means the אדרכתא from the last step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on when the ninety-day wait applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the borrower refuses to come, the אדרכתא is written immediately.

steps.title: No waiting for a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The waiting periods apply only to a loan. For a פקדון, the אדרכתא is written immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies to a loan. But for a deposit, we write it immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a second limit: the ninety-day wait is only for loans, not for deposits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a loan, the borrower spent the money and may need time to raise it. With a פקדון, the guardian is supposed to still have the item in hand, so there is no reason to give him time.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit left with a guardian for safekeeping

steps.whatToRemember: A שטר can be confirmed without the borrower present. He still gets time to bring witnesses, then Monday-Thursday-Monday, then a ninety-day ban, and only then an אדרכתא. All this waiting is skipped if he says 'I am not coming,' or if the case is a פקדון rather than a loan.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the court balances moving the case forward with fairness to the defendant. It waits only when there is a real reason to expect he needs time.

phrases.english: And this applies to a loan,
but with a deposit, we write it immediately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second limit on the ninety-day wait, after the 'I am not coming' limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The waiting periods apply only to loans. For a פקדון, the אדרכתא is written immediately.

steps.title: The document is written only on land, not on movable property
steps.stepSummary: An אדרכתא is written only on the borrower's land. Movables are left out, because the lender might use them up, and then the borrower would have nothing to collect back if he later proves the שטר is no good.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we write an אדרכתא, it covers land, not movable things. Maybe the lender will grab the movables and use them up. Then, when the borrower comes with witnesses and breaks the שטר, he will find nothing to collect back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to the אדרכתא from the last steps: it can only cover the borrower's land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower may still come back with witnesses and show the שטר is not valid. Land stays where it is and can be returned. Movables can be eaten, sold or lost, so the borrower could be left with nothing to recover.

keyTerms.meaning: Weakens or breaks the validity of the document

phrases.english: And when we write [an אדרכתא], it is on land,
phrases.notes: The אדרכתא is the court's permission to seize the borrower's property.

phrases.english: but on movable property, no;
perhaps he will grab and use them up,
the lender, the movable property,
and when the borrower comes and brings witnesses
and breaks the document,
he will not find anything to collect.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי כָּתְבִינַן – אַמְּקַרְקְעֵי, אֲבָל אַמִּטַּלְטְלִי – לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit on which property the אדרכתא from steps 19-21 may cover.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אדרכתא is written on land only, not on movables, so that the borrower can still recover if the שטר is later broken.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the court protecting the borrower even while it lets the lender collect.

steps.title: A suggested exception when the lender owns land
steps.stepSummary: A suggestion: if the lender has land of his own, the court may write the אדרכתא even on movables, because the borrower could collect back from the lender's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the lender has land, we do write it, even on movables.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests an exception to the rule just given. This sets up the next step, which will reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry in step 22 was that the borrower would have nothing to collect back. If the lender owns land, the borrower could collect from that land, so the worry seems to go away.

keyTerms.meaning: We write (the court issues the document)

phrases.english: And if the lender has land,
we write [it, even on movables].

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִית לֵיהּ מְקַרְקְעֵי לְמַלְוֶה – כָּתְבִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an exception based on the reason given in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lender owns land, the אדרכתא may be written on movables as well. Step 24 rejects this.

steps.title: Rejected: the lender's land might lose value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggested exception. No אדרכתא is written on movables even if the lender owns land, because his land could go down in value.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is not so. We do not write an אדרכתא on movables, even if the lender has land, because we worry the land may lose value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the exception from step 23 with the words ולא היא, "that is not so."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Owning land today does not guarantee the borrower will be fully paid back later. The land might get worse and be worth less than the movables the lender used up. So the basic rule from step 22 stands with no exception.

keyTerms.meaning: "But that is not so," a formula that rejects a view just stated
Lose value, get worse (literally, grow pale)

steps.whatToRemember: An אדרכתא never covers movables, not even when the lender owns land.

phrases.english: But that is not so;
we do not write an אדרכתא on movable property,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית לֵיהּ מְקַרְקְעֵי;
phrases.english: even though he [the lender] has land;
we are concerned that it may lose value.
phrases.notes: "It" is the lender's land. Literally the word means "grow pale," so the land may get worse and be worth less.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the exception proposed in step 23.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole exception for a lender who owns land.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumes the lender's land will keep its value, but land can lose value.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An אדרכתא is never written on movables.

steps.title: The borrower is notified first, but only if he is nearby
steps.stepSummary: Before writing an אדרכתא, the court lets the borrower know. This applies only when he lives nearby, not when he is far away.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we write an אדרכתא, we let him know. This applies when he is nearby, but if he is far away, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a new rule: the court warns the borrower before writing the אדרכתא, but only if he is close by.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Telling him gives him one last chance to pay or to answer the claim. If he is far away, sending word is not practical, so the court does not wait for that.

keyTerms.meaning: "And these words apply only...", a formula that limits a rule

phrases.english: And when we write an אדרכתא,
we inform him.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the borrower, the one whose property is about to be taken.

phrases.english: And this applies only when he is nearby,
but if he is far away, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which property the אדרכתא covers to how the court issues it: first notifying the borrower.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court notifies a nearby borrower before writing an אדרכתא, but does not notify one who is far away.

steps.title: A distant borrower with a way to be reached: wait twelve months
steps.stepSummary: If the borrower is far away but has relatives nearby, or caravans travel to his place and back, the court waits twelve months so a caravan can go and return.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is far away but there are relatives, or there are caravans that go there and come back, we wait twelve months, until the caravan goes and comes back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes the rule in step 25 more precise. A far-away borrower who can still be reached gets a twelve-month wait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The "far away, no" rule in step 25 is for a borrower with no way to be reached. If relatives or caravans can bring him word, the court gives the message time to get to him and get back.

keyTerms.meaning: The twelve months of the year

phrases.english: And if he is far away but there are relatives,
or if there are caravans
that go and come back from there,
we wait for him the twelve months of the year
until the caravan goes and comes back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי מְרַחַק וְאִיכָּא קְרוֹבִים, אִי נָמֵי אִיכָּא שְׁיָירָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the "far away, no" part of step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A far-away borrower who can be reached through relatives or caravans gets a twelve-month wait before the אדרכתא is written.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read step 25 as "anyone far away is never notified." It only means someone who cannot be reached at all.

steps.title: The case of רבינא and מר אחא supports the twelve-month wait
steps.stepSummary: רבינא waited twelve months in a case for מר אחא, until a caravan went to בי חוזאי and came back. This shows the rule in action.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the case where רבינא waited twelve months for מר אחא, until a caravan went to and came back from בי חוזאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the twelve-month rule with a real case judged by רבינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story matches the rule exactly: a twelve-month delay timed to a caravan going to a far place and returning. It shows this was actually done in court.

keyTerms.meaning: "Like this case of...", a formula that brings a story as support

steps.whatToRemember: Notify a nearby borrower before writing the אדרכתא. Do not hold onto the twelve-month wait as the rule, because the next step rejects it with וְלָא הִיא.

phrases.english: Like this case of רבינא,

phrases.aramaic: שְׁהָא לְמָר אַחָא תְּרֵיסַר יַרְחֵי שַׁתָּא,
phrases.english: who waited for מר אחא the twelve months of the year,

phrases.aramaic: עַד דְּאָזְלָא וְאָתְיָיא שְׁיָירָא מִבֵּי חוֹזָאֵי.
phrases.english: until a caravan went to and came back from בי חוזאי.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרָבִינָא שְׁהָא לְמָר אַחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real case that supports the rule in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: The twelve-month wait for a far-away borrower who can be reached by caravan.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case judged by רבינא for מר אחא, involving a caravan to בי חוזאי.

steps.title: The twelve-month wait was a special case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the general twelve-month waiting rule. רבינא waited only because the lender was violent. Normally the court waits only as long as a one-day trip.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not so. In that case the man was violent. If he got the אדרכתא into his hands, nobody could take it back from him. But in an ordinary case, we wait only long enough for a messenger to go on Tuesday, for the borrower to come on Wednesday, and for him to stand trial on Thursday.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the twelve-month rule from the last steps is wrong. רבינא's long wait happened only because of an unusual, dangerous lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 seemed to prove that the court waits twelve months for a borrower who is far away. Here the גמרא explains that case differently. The lender was violent, so once he held an אדרכתא it could never be taken back from him, and extra caution was needed. In a normal case the court waits only for a borrower who can be reached and brought in within about a day.

keyTerms.meaning: But that is not so: a rejection of what was just said

steps.whatToRemember: The court does not normally wait twelve months. It waits only if the borrower can be told and can come within about a day. רבינא's twelve-month wait was a special case because of a violent lender.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not leave this section thinking the twelve-month wait is the rule. The words וְלָא הִיא overturn that conclusion.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule for how long a בית דין delays an אדרכתא for a borrower who is not present.

phrases.english: But that is not so;
there, he was a violent man,
phrases.notes: "There" points back to רבינא's case for מר אחא, and the violent man is the lender.

phrases.english: if an authorization document reached his hands,
it would not be possible to take it back from him.
But here, we do not wait for him

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַד דְּאָזֵיל שְׁלִיחָא בִּתְלָתָא בְּשַׁבְּתָא
phrases.english: except until a messenger goes on Tuesday
and he comes on Wednesday,
and on Thursday he stands trial.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the twelve-month rule that step 27 seemed to prove, and explains רבינא's case as special.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The general rule of waiting twelve months for a far-away borrower who has relatives nearby or whose town caravans reach.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבינא's case had a special reason, the violent lender, so it cannot teach a general rule.

steps.title: The court's messenger is believed like two witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules that the messenger of the חכמים is believed like two witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The messenger of the חכמים is believed by us as if he were two witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has just mentioned a court messenger, so it now brings a new rule from רבינא about how far such a messenger is trusted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually two witnesses are needed to establish a fact. Here one court messenger is trusted that much, for example when he reports that the person refused to come to court. The next step limits this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The messenger sent by the חכמים, meaning the court

phrases.english: Ravina said:
This messenger of the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: This is the messenger the court sends to call someone to come before it.

phrases.english: we believe him like two witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up on the messenger mentioned in step 28 and opens a new topic about how far he is trusted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court's messenger is believed like two witnesses.

steps.title: The messenger is trusted for שמתא but not for פתיחא
steps.stepSummary: The messenger's trust applies to a שמתא, but not to a פתיחא, because a פתיחא costs the person money for the scribe.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to a שמתא. But for a פתיחא, the messenger is not believed. A פתיחא causes the person a loss of money, because he has to pay the scribe who writes it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits רבינא's rule. The messenger is fully trusted only for a שמתא, not for a written פתיחא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פתיחא is a written document, and the person has to pay the scribe for it. Because the messenger's word would cost him real money, one messenger is not enough. A שמתא carries no such cost, so for a שמתא the messenger is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: And this applies only to: a phrase that limits a rule
A ban spoken by the court
A written document of a ban

steps.confusionAlert: שמתא and פתיחא are not the same. A שמתא is spoken, while a פתיחא is written and costs money. That difference is the whole reason for this limit.

phrases.english: And this applies to excommunication,
but for a written document of ban,
since it causes him a loss of money,
because he must give
money to the scribe, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבינא's rule from step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The messenger is believed for a שמתא but not for a פתיחא, since a פתיחא causes a loss of money.

steps.title: A court date may be passed on through a woman or neighbors
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules that a summons to court may be passed on through a woman or through neighbors.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: We may set a court date for a person by telling it to a woman or to his neighbors.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives another rule about calling someone to court. The message does not have to be given to him directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court may give the message to a woman or to the person's neighbors, and they are trusted to pass it along. The next step limits when this is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A set date to appear in court

phrases.english: Ravina said:
We give a court date
by word of a woman and by word of neighbors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another rule from רבינא about calling a person to court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A court date may be passed on through a woman or through neighbors.

steps.title: Only when he is not in town
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the rule. A summons through a woman or neighbors works only when the person is not in town.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said this only when he is not in the town.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to limit רבינא's rule. Passing the message through others applies only when the person himself is out of town. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person is in town, the court can reach him directly, so it does not rely on others to pass the message along. The rule about a woman or neighbors is meant for when he is away.

keyTerms.meaning: We said this only: a phrase that limits a rule
He is not in the town

phrases.english: And we said this only
when he is not in the town,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבינא's rule from step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A summons through a woman or neighbors applies only when the person is not in town.
